utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, ma'am. All the accused are here. The composition is the same as yesterday with the exception of Mr. Josse and Mr. Lazarevic that I don't see unless the column is in the way. Okay. So the understanding is, and correct me if I am wrong, that the Popovic defence team has decided to reduce the cross-examination from eight hours to two hours and that the Nikolic defence team has increased its request from about 45 minutes to about one hour today; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stick to the one hour, please, Mr. Bourgon and good afternoon to you, and good afternoon to you, Mr. Pandurevic. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Judges, good afternoon, colleagues, and good afternoon, sir. If I could have in e-court, please, 3D444.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that we looked at yesterday and I just have one quick question. If you can read the first page of this document, the first paragraph where it says: "In addition to information submitted previously, our associate Zmaj has told us the following ..." I would just like to confirm that you know that Zmaj was a Muslim that was used as a secret source by 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic to obtain intelligence information on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard the code-name before, the way it's written here. If you say that he was a Muslim forwarding information to Nikolic then that must be true. I can't confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, then, can you confirm, sir, that you were aware that Drago Nikolic was using secret sources to obtain intelligence information of which you would be made aware?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had any persons on the Muslim side working with him, forwarding this sort of information to him. Perhaps he did, it's just that he never told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well that's exactly my question, sir. It says here: "In addition to information submitted previously, our associate Zmaj ..." is it your testimony today that you were never informed that Drago Nikolic was using associates as they are referred to in this report, to obtain intelligence information of which you would be made aware?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand the methods that they used in their work, he would never disclose to anyone his network of associates. This information is about the Sekovac Brigade and the Vis [phoen] facility which was in their defence zone. Perhaps he received information from them and perhaps he obtained information himself from another source, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once again, sir that's not my question. Were you made aware that Drago Nikolic used associates or secret sources to obtain intelligence information that you were made aware of while you were brigade commander whether it's a Muslim or any other associates?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you he probably had sources, I didn't know who the people were or their whereabouts. I received information as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So then when you saw this report here associate Zmaj you never asked any question, Who is Zmaj?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why the word itself strikes me itself as strange, Zmaj. I had never noticed that word before so I'm asking myself if I had ever heard the code-name used before in the context of this report which doesn't necessarily imply that he did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying, sir. Did you hear of any other code names of associates used by Drago Nikolic, and he would say, I've obtained this information which I'm telling you today from one of my associates and provide you with the name of the associates?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he ever mentioned the names of his associates to me. The usual thing to do was to say source reliable, information verified, or non-verified and that was the extent of what I would normally learn about a source.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question on this document. Look down to the before-last paragraph, I hope you have the same in your language, if I can have -- yes, you do where it says: "The associate was inserted back into enemy territory in the evening of 10 May 1995. His next entry back into our territory is scheduled for the evening of 14 May 1994." So you're telling us that you never had information like this from Drago Nikolic during the time you were commander of the Zvornik Brigade; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I don't know whether I ever learned those. I don't remember. He would have had to forward this type of information to me. That much is true but I'm telling you about the sources. He certainly was not disclosing his sources to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll say again, sir. Did you, while you were brigade commander, did Drago Nikolic come to you and say, I obtained this information from one of my associates and he gave you that intelligence information, whether in writing or orally? Did that happen or did that never happen, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, he did forward information to me, but he would not specify the source. Sometimes he would forward to me information that had arrived from the corps, generally speaking, regrettably, the Army of Republika Srpska, the Drina Corps specifically as far as I know, did not always have the right information and did not always know in time what the enemy's intentions were. This was one of our weaknesses that marked us throughout the war, poor intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, sir. When Drago Nikolic provided you information, did he tell you that he had information coming from secret sources and he gave you what the information was? Did he or did he not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the third time, he did forward information to me, but I did not know the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court, please, 3D529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session and wait until you -- I give you the go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just out of an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Wait until I give you the go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason why I'm saying this, it was explained to me yesterday that since the order is to be translated, sometimes it happens that we switch on from one mode to the other prematurely. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report on the combat readiness of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade for the period of 1 January until 31 December 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document yet. Here it is. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, one of the purpose of this report is to review the activities in which the Zvornik Brigade was involved during 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the date this was done, the 27th of January, 1995. I was not there then, I was receiving treatment elsewhere. This was supposed to be an analysis of combat readiness and not a report on the situation in relation to combat readiness. That's how the title should have read, in relation to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen this type of document before for other years at any time, and does it normally include a review of the main activities conducted by the brigade in the previous year?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Analyses are conducted on a yearly or bi-yearly basis depending on the level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this report also provides the status of the brigade in terms of combat readiness as of the end of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in relation to 1994 in it's entirety. This is an analysis of combat readiness according to each of its elements. There is a standard form that is used and the elements recur every year virtually across the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Another objective of this report is to highlight if, as of the end of 1994, there are any problems which need to be resolved in order to increase the combat readiness of the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the analysis is to review the overall situation, to analyse the strengths and the weaknesses, spotting workable solutions, spotting omissions, shortcomings, weaknesses and taking measures to enhance the level of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court, please, page 15 of this document in English and page 17 in B/C/S. The last page of the document in B/C/S. Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you can confirm that this document was compiled and signed by your Chief of Staff Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was compiled by Miodrag Dragutinovic, typed up by Misko Vasic, and signed by Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can also confirm that when the Chief of Staff of the brigade prepares this document, he draws from and calls upon the officers working in the command staff working under his direction as well as his three assistant commanders to provide him to with the necessary information, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a simplification of the entire process, an over simplification, actually. The commander's signature should have been here indicating that I was there at the time or in this case deputy commander Major Dragan Obrenovic. As for the analysis, it is conducted based on a special plan in addition to the commander and the Chief of Staff the persons involved are the assistants certain officers from the operative organ and normally the commanders of subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again, sir, that was not my question. I was not describing the process, I was asking: Are the officers working in the command and your three assistant commanders involved; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that's what I said right now, Mr. Bourgon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in English page 12, and in B/C/S, page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you see on this page the section of the report called "Intelligence and Security Support." Would you agree with me that in this section, it would have been compiled and drafted by 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic as the assistant commander for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been the one compiling this report but the combat readiness category contains this element called security. Intelligence is not an element of combat readiness but because of some of the details to do with the establishment at the time, the whole thing was mixed up somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, you will agree with me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this section here, section 6, and maybe we can go to the next page because I'm told that there is a difference between the English and the B/C/S. If I can have the next page in B/C/S, please, so that we get the full title, intelligence and security support.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should go back, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, if we can go back to the previous page in B/C/S. Sir, this contains a review of the activities conducted within the intelligence and security organ during the year 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, I'll just ask you to draw your attention to a few lines in this document, and the first one I'd like to -- is to the sentence which begins with: "Reconnaissance of the enemy," that's in subparagraph A, the second paragraph, where it says: "Reconnaissance of the enemy has been carried out in force according to the plans of the brigade command and battalion commands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, next page in B/C/S, please, second paragraph. Just above the 6 where it says: "Reconnaissance of the enemy has been carried out in force according to the plans of the brigade command and battalion commands."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you read this sentence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you've got that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you do because it's the paragraph just above --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the last line of this paragraph reads, you can read that with me: "All intelligence data has been delivered to users regularly in duty." Did you read this part of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now I draw your attention to subparagraph B where it says "security support." I will read this paragraph and -- which reads as follows: "Great attention is given to counter-intelligence work. Particular attention is devoted to preventing leaks of secret military information. For this reason, 6 hand-held radios ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It should be there in both languages, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay it's okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: "Six hand-held radios were confiscated from persons talking to the Turks on the so-called hot line." Do you see this, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a little further down, I draw your attention to where it says, the paragraph beginning with: "During the year we had one case where soldiers in the 4th Battalion zone of responsibility had direct contact with the Turks. Reaction was swift and further contact was prevented on the same day. There is nothing to indicate that there have been such contacts in other units, but it is common for soldiers to shout across the lines and talk to the Turks. This phenomenon should be energetically discouraged." The last sentence reads: "All data collected by counter-intelligence work is duly delivered to users." Have you read this paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I draw your attention a little bit further down, the paragraph that deals with the military police. It says, and you can read from this paragraph beginning with "in the brigade ..." all the way down to the last where it says attachment number 16. Do you agree that in this paragraph, it says that requests were received to take into custody the word used here in the English version is "to bring in" 3.369 men from the Zvornik Brigade and 821 men from other brigades. It also says, amongst other things, that 2.911 men from the Zvornik Brigade were, in fact, taken into custody and that 211 were kept into custody. Do you see this information, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You will agree with me that these are activities which would involve some sort of supervision by 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course he had to do something that was part of his job. You see that he is here directly reporting on what the police did and how many people were brought in. He talks about the problems regarding command and control and a number of other problems too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, on the basis of the information we just reviewed together, those lines that we read together in this report, I put it to you that it is simply incorrect to say that 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic was performing tasks under your control for only 20 percent of the time; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ever since the two bodies were separated, that was certainly true. In 1995, it was 20 percent under my orders. In relation to this period, one couldn't state the same thing because both bodies were still joined. However, this sabotage and reconnaissance platoon was under the command of the Chief of Staff. This is an annual overview of the activities. It was never the case that, for example, our reconnaissance group was infiltrated deep into enemy territory. There was always a scout in a trench with a pair of binoculars observing what was going on and that was all the intelligence activity that he ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It appears to me that this is a change in your testimony as well as not a real answer to the question I was asking; however, I'll ask you a new one. In light of this information, and especially both lines where it says that all data collected by intelligence has been delivered to users regularly and duly and the fact that all data collected by counter-intelligence work is duly delivered to users, that it is simply incorrect to say that you were not kept aware of all information you needed to command the Zvornik Brigade by 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic; is that true, sir? A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is what true? Is it true that it is a change in his testimony? Is it true that it's not an answer to the question he was asked? Is it true to any of the following six questions that appear in that paragraph. What is the question there? It's not fair on the witness to just to say is that true at the end of a speech like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I appreciate the tag team, they know that the time is counted, I appreciate it, I have no problem with that; that's fair game, but let me be very, very clear. There are two sentences there in this report that I read. I read those two sentences with the witness: All intelligence data has been delivered to users, all counter-intelligence data has been delivered to users. And we've covered that it's a report prepared by the Chief of Staff Obrenovic, and he said that it's a report that he should have signed and I suggest to him on the basis of these two sentences that it is not true that he was not being kept informed of everything by Drago Nikolic. It's a very simple question, and he can answer yes or he can deny it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the way you have condensed it now into one question, namely whether it's true that he, in other words, whether it's true that it's not correct to say that he was not kept aware of all the information he needed to command the Zvornik Brigade by the 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic, I think he can answer that now. It's being put to you that what you've previously stated is not correct and that, in other words, you were kept aware of all information you needed to command the Zvornik Brigade by Accused Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer that one, Your Honours. We're looking at a theory here that counter-intelligence was duly and timely forwarded to users, but we don't see the word "commanders" there. We should see what sort of counter-intelligence we're looking at and then throughout this trial we have arrived at the conclusion that counter-intelligence was forwarded to a commander only to the extent that the security organ believed was necessary. But they certainly were forwarding all their counter-intelligence to their superior security organ which doesn't necessarily mean that all of Drago Nikolic's counter-intelligence was available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, in all this report which covers the entire year 1994, there is not one line that indicates that there was any type of problem where the commander felt he was not getting the information he needed; is that true or is that not true?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this kind of report is drafting as a template. If we leave out some specific information and figure, it might relate to any brigade within the Army of Republika Srpska. It does not mention any problems of which there were many, and therefore, this is not a good report because it does not contain a critical analysis of the work of this organ. This is just a cosmetic touches on how the work was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir that's like your combat report of 16 July, it is inaccurate and you provided inaccurate information to the corps command where you had problems with Drago Nikolic, and you did not put it in that report. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no problems with Drago Nikolic on the 16th, I didn't even see him. I don't know where he was or what he was doing, or whether he had any problems himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe it's a question of translation. I'm not talking about the 16th. I'm talking this is another report where you provide false information to the corps command because it's your testimony that there were problems with Drago Nikolic and you did not put that in that report. Is that your testimony or the fact that the report does not contain a line shown that there were no problems. Which one of the two is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 6 was drafted by Drago Nikolic and handed over to Mijo Dragutinovic. Being an operative, he combined it. And put it together. This was neither written by Dragutinovic, Obrenovic, or myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is it a report approved by the brigade by whoever and sent to the corps command; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court, please, 3D443.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, the document that will appear before you is the brigade monthly work plan of the Zvornik Brigade command for the month of July 1995. Do you recognise this type -- this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this kind of documents, may even probably have even this one while it was being drafted, but I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And these documents were drafted for every month for the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And they were drafted by the Chief of Staff at least one month in advance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the date, 31st of May is incorrect whereas the next month as it says here is July. The schedule is being normally done at the end of the current month for the next month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the date at the top corner in the left 30 June 1995, would be the correct date for this document for the upcoming month of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The print is too small, I can't see whether it is the 30th of June or ... yes, it says the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If I can have page 2 in both B/C/S and English, please. And on this page 2, sir, I will draw your attention to number 8 where it says: "Protect units from enemy intelligence and reconnaissance activities." Sir, you will agree with me that this was one of the focal tasks as it says here, of the Zvornik Brigade, for the month of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, more or less the tasks didn't vary throughout the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court, please, page 4 in English and page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you are familiar with this type of report. I'd just like you to confirm where the columns at the top say "tasks to be carried out by," and before there is a column for cooperating. That simply means exactly what it says; there's a person responsible for the task and there are other persons or other organs cooperating in the task; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever is written here is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were the commander in 1995, I'm asking you to confirm; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, everywhere on this document where we see chief of security or PKBO for assistant commander for security and intelligence, everywhere we see these two terms, this would be a task either to be carried out by Drago Nikolic or in which Drago Nikolic was involved as your intelligence -- your security organ.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like, please, to see the page where the tasks of security organs are displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: By all means, sir. I refer to page 8 in English -- page 12 in English and the corresponding page in B/C/S where the numbers 62 to 71 appear. So it would be page 7 in B/C/S. Now again that was not my question but you see here there is a section 7, or 6 for security organ. And you see in the box where task to be performed by, you see chief of security. And the task where we see at line 71, we see OBO, that's also your organ of security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from item 70 all the way to item 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if I look at item 72, for example, it says "briefing by the chief of brigade security and corps command." Those are briefings. And it says here, "OBO," which means that this is a task for which the security organ was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a combination of his tasks relating to security, counter-intelligence, and police work as well as his obligations vis-a-vis the command corps and -- corps command and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, you will agree with me that during that period for the month of July 1995, 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic was regularly assigned as brigade operations duty officer both at the brigade command and at the brigade forward command post. Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can in e-court, please, 3D435.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, the document that will appear before you is a security measures plan and it says, as you will see in the top left corner, "Approved by the brigade commander." And you will agree with me -- well, maybe we have the wrong document. 435, 3D435. You will see in the top left corner that this security plan is approved by the brigade commander and that the code-name is Stit 95; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention something about this yesterday. This is one of the attachment with the commander's order. This was supposed to be approved by the commander, however, there is no handwritten signature and this is one of the staff documents of the security organ, and it was his duty to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So this document, sir, was attached to the order, signed by the commander, but because there's no signature, it's not approved by you; is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the commander's decision, attachments are compiled such as chief of various branches issue orders for their respective area, the same applies to the security organ, the moral guidance organ, the intelligence organs, et cetera, do their own share. All has to tally with the commander's order or decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as brigade commander, did you ensure that they tallied with your order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this Operation Stit. I didn't participate in the compilation thereof, but the commander should know whether all the elements are in compliance with his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir this is for 1995 and it's not an operation but it's a plan you can see; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a plan of security measure as part of the combat plan or the wartime engagement of the Drina Corps. All these documents were drafted under code-name Stit 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have page 2 in B/C/S and English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when you look at this page 2, maybe we can just put that in -- because I need the witness to see the columns. Sir, we see that this is a number of tasks which all are tasks to be performed by 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic in 1995 in coordination with various other organs in the brigade command and battalions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this document shows the relationship which should exist between the commander and the assistant commander for security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on the basis of the documents that we've reviewed together, the brigade monthly plan for 1995, the security plan for Stit in 1995, as well as the previous document we looked at, so that's what I want, my question will be focussing on those three documents that we looked at. And here is my question: On this basis, I put it to you that other than for the fact that you discovered that 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic provided information about you to the corps command security chief, there were absolutely no problems between yourself and your assistant commander for security in 1995; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have seen that the problems go back to 1994 whereas the plan that we see now and other similar plans were exactly the reason for misunderstanding. A lot of things were put on paper but not implemented. Once I insist on this being implemented, then it is construed as my meddling with the security issues. If you are familiar with security operation, you would know where his 80 percent engagement is and where the other 20 percent of his engagement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, you mentioned that you complained or you asked the corps commander for direction as to how to employ your assistant commander for security, Drago Nikolic. I'd like to know when you contacted the corps commander, who you spoke to, and what you were told exactly.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't seek guidelines from the corps commander for how to engage Drago Nikolic. Instead, I asked the corps commander to inform me that his assistant for security had planned to engage Drago Nikolic and that was all. It happened on a few occasions throughout the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In writing or orally, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to a different topic which is my last one. You can confirm that the commander of the military police company was Jasikovac within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And correct me if I am wrong, but you've said that when it comes to the use of the military police company in combat, this has nothing to do with Drago Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not within his mandate, but if he is given an order to command this company, he may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, in fact, the use of the military police in combat is a command decision can only be taken by yourself or by someone standing in by you such as, for example, your Chief of Staff acting as deputy commander in your absence; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because that was not the basic or the fundamental purpose of engaging the police and that is in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, I take it that this is what you were referring to when you said, and I quote from page 30765, line 13 to 30766, line 9: "In practical terms as your Chief of Staff or chief of -- if your Chief of Staff or chief of security wanted to employ some military policemen, would you necessarily be consulted about that?" Your answer was: "Since all of these headquarters support units are units attached to the staff" -- just one moment, please. I was just trying to read a shorter quote to try to save some time. It starts at line 22 of what I just said and it reads as follows: "In the case of the police and in the case of counter-intelligence work and the need in the course of such work to involve the police or to use some kind of equipment well in such a case I would not have been informed of the matter; but if it was necessary to use the police company to carry out a particular task, or if it was necessary to use a platoon from that company, I or someone standing in for me would have been asked to authorise such a task." Now, having read your testimony, I'm simply saying that if the military police is to be used in combat, that this falls in the category of particular task which can only be approved by you or someone standing in for you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If there is an emergency situation and the use of police cannot be avoided, Drago could have issued an order to that effect, but then he would be obliged to later inform the commander about having used such a unit in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have P322 in e-court, page 1 in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's look at an example, sir. You will see a document which you've seen before during this trial, it's a regular combat report dated 12 July 1995 from the command of the Zvornik Brigade and addressed to the command of the Drina Corps. I draw your attention to paragraph 2 where it says that one military police platoon will set an ambush at Dzafin Kamen by 1700 hours. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that Drago Nikolic would have had nothing to do with the sending the military police platoon to Dzafin Kamen?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should have been a decision to take -- to be taken by Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And further down on this document, it says: "One military police detachment was sent to Konjevic Polje pursuant to your order." Do you see this, and in the meantime can I go in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir we also know from the evidence that Drago Nikolic was not on duty on the 12 of July and that he had the day off; do you recall this evidence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that specific date but this is an example how command functions should function. The command corps -- corps command issues an order to the brigade command which could have been forwarded to the company commander of Jasikovac or Nikolic, I don't know who the command was forwarded to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you said that you were familiar with the evidence that we just reviewed in private session. What I'm telling you today is that even if Drago Nikolic had been at the command on that day, you will agree with me that he could not send the military police detachment without seeking the authorisation of the Chief of Staff who was then acting as deputy commander in your absence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff or rather my deputy received this order, and he told either Drago Nikolic or Jasikovac to send this police squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question was: Drago Nikolic could not have done so without seeking the authorisation from the Chief of Staff who was standing in for you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could he have done if he hadn't received such an order and he has no knowledge of what he is supposed to do with them and where to send them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if the Chief of Staff is present in the brigade command and the brigade operations duty officer, whoever he is, received this order from the corps command, he doesn't give it to Drago Nikolic, he gives it to the Chief of Staff who is the one who can authorise the deployment of this detachment to Konjevic Polje; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if he hadn't -- had been here, it could have been forwarded to Drago Nikolic or Jasikovac, and they would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is because if the Chief of Staff had not been there, the brigade duty operations officer would then have taken a decision which would be a command decision on behalf of the commander of the brigade; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wouldn't take a decision but rather relay the order from the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can in e-court, please, 3D340.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, the document that will appear before you is an order issued by yourself on 18 March 1995. And the topic of the order as you will see, is prevention of desertion and uncontrolled draining away from soldiers -- away of soldiers from units, do you see this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You agree that preventing desertion or dealing with soldiers that desert falls within the remit of 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was first and foremost the responsibility of the commanders of the units from which these soldiers have deserted; however, if that happened, then a military police company is engaged to locate these men and gather them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as such, is that included within the remit of Drago Nikolic's responsibilities because he supervises the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I commanded the police through him. He issued them with specific tasks and pursuant to this order, it was his duty to make arrangements for what is stipulated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I take good note of what you just mentioned that you commanded the military police through Drago Nikolic, but I ask you to look at paragraph 1 through this order where it says that 12 soldiers from the military police company are to establish checkpoints in three different places on 25 -- by 25 March 1995. And those places are well identified in this paragraph. Then it says that the exact location of the checkpoint is to be decided by the chief of security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I could have page 2 in B/C/S and English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, here we see in paragraph 6 of this order -- can you see paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have this moved to the right slightly, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So we see that for the implementation of this order, you hold the brigade chief of security as well as the assistant Chief of Staff for personnel and legal affairs responsible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant Chief of Staff for personnel. That's how it should read, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you on the basis of this order that 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic could not, by himself, select 12 members of the military police company and set up these checkpoints without an order from you or your approval; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he produced a proposal on how many soldiers would be required and where the points, the checkpoints would be. So then I looked at the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the proposal was approved by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you know our position in this case which is that Drago Nikolic never requested the Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic, to have members of the military police company be put at his disposal in the evening of 13 July. That's our case, and we've made our case very clear. Nonetheless, my question is the following: You will agree with me that even if Drago Nikolic had made such a request to the Chief of Staff, who was acting as deputy commander in your absence in the evening of 13 July, what I'm putting to you is that the information contained in the statement of facts of Dragan Obrenovic concerning the request he would have received from Drago Nikolic, that makes it clear that 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic could not have used members of the military police that night for the purpose of observing the arrival of the convoy of prisoners without first seeking the approval of the Chief of Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a lengthy question. You say he didn't request that and now, as far as I understand, you say he couldn't take it and he didn't request that. Based on what I know about the statements made by Dragan Obrenovic, he did make the request, and the request was approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I do apologise, it's my last question. I'm done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I do admit that this question was very long. I will try to make it very simple. You've just mentioned that on the basis of the evidence, Drago Nikolic would have requested the military police to place at his disposal. But I'm saying to you that that night, whether he did or not, he could not do so, he could not use those military police to attend the arrival of any prisoners at any time without seeking the approval of the Chief of Staff. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He could have done it anyway. If, for example, he hadn't found the Chief of Staff anywhere around, he certainly would have done it nevertheless. You look at all the documents in this trial where tasks are given to the military police directly by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, can you point to some of these documents, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the document numbers off the top of my head, but I'm sure they are bound to turn up again sometime during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We'll have a -- we'll come back to you in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, both Mr. Josse and Mr. Lazarevic are now present. Now, I take it you are next, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I give you the floor, I just want to check with the rest of you for a revised assessment. Mr. Ostojic, you had asked for eight and a half hours. What's your assessment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately eight hours, Mr. President, but I will try to endeavour to shorten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Gosnell, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've just sent an e-mail indicating that we're increasing our estimate from 30 minutes to one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had we known that, Mr. Bourgon, we wouldn't have extended. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for the time being, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's every chance we will ask no questions, but we would like to reserve the 30 minutes we had previously asked for, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey, you are still tied to your 20 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's going to be, after the last cross, there's certain areas I'm not going to have to get into with the kind of detail we just saw, so I know it will be less than 20. How much, I don't really know quite yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, Mr. Haynes, where is Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming back to you on the short break that you had asked for upon the termination of your client's testimony with a view to reviewing the list of witnesses to follow. You had asked for a week at some point in time and my understanding is that you would still like a week. My suggestion to you is I'm sure you can achieve the same result, be able to get to a conclusion if we give you two or three days? We find it difficult to grant one whole week for the purpose that you have indicated. Especially since we have been hearing evidence for 13 or 14 days already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The principal difficulty is, of course, that we are all creatures of our instructions and all the decisions we have to take have to be taken in consultation with Mr. Pandurevic from whom we are maintaining a healthy distance at the moment. We're keeping an eye on his health and welfare, but other than that, we are fastidiously observing the limitation that you placed upon our contact with him. And if we are only to have two or three days after the conclusion of his evidence, we are simply not going to be able to go through with him the decisions that we have to take. There are 23 witnesses other than him on our 65 ter list, 686 documents; eight witnesses are scheduled for the month of March with whom we propose to consider 534 documents. We have to provide the victims and witnesses service with a minimum of five days' notice of witnesses we propose to bring next month, and we're getting very close to end of this month. Monday is the 21st, and realistically we would have to make that decision by Tuesday for March witnesses. So it's not, in our view, an outrageous request. We make it on the basis that we want to be in proper and full consultation with our client. We don't want to cause inconvenience with the victims and witnesses section, and we don't want to be in a position where we are a causing witnesses to be brought here next Tuesday that we later decide we're not going to call and cause immense cost and inconvenience to those people, not cost to those people, but cost to the Tribunal. So I do submit that a working week is necessary for that process and to avoid time wastage later on and unnecessary inconvenience to the organs of the Tribunal and to any witnesses we would wish to call -- would wish to cancel or what have you. Sorry, that was rather inelegant. If, however, you are against me on that we may as well seek your leave to start discussing those matters with Mr. Pandurevic now, which I don't want to do, not least because he's undergoing an extremely tiring procedure anyway, and I prefer to leave him to rest for the rest of the day that he's not giving evidence. But that's our position for what it's worth. I know I would be roundly supported in that if you threw the floor open but I don't think, on the pure basis of my submissions, I can expand any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And just to get a clearer picture, I would imagine you would have a re-examination, re-direct? How long would you, given the situation as it stands now, how long would you expect that to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not a great believer in re-examination, but there are certain things already that I would like to sweep up. I'd have thought it might take a day, a working day, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Having heard you, we'll come back to you. Yes, I'll come back to you -- do you wish to comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. The Prosecution does support that. We would benefit by a break of a week to get ourselves together and prepare for the future and maybe able to discuss things with Mr. Haynes and see if I can help to convince him to streamline what he is doing. So given the process that we're going now and how much exertion is going on, I think a week is not inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you be agreeable to Mr. Pandurevic meeting with his client to discuss -- to discuss only these matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's no problem and next week is also "crocus vakantie," so it's a very important week in Holland to take off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's also carnival. Mr. Ostojic, in case Mr. Haynes can conduct these discussions with his client over the weekend, for example, since you wouldn't be finished with your cross-examination, would you be against Mr. Haynes meeting with his client to discuss these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll come back to -- yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I thought I should just point out that meeting my client over the weekend is not possible under the rules of the detention unit, he's only allowed social visits at the weekends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't he meet his counsel socially?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Well, if you're going to grant him provisional release. I won't stand in your way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come back to you tomorrow on this. Now, Mr. McCloskey, you realise that time is of the essence now. We are very fastly approaching the end of the last of the defence cases, and we are concerned about two things. First is the following: You will recall that we had granted a motion some time back for you to reopen the Prosecution case and you had indicated at the time, in your 7th April motion that you estimate that testimony to last for about two and three quarters hours, roughly three hours, 2.75 hours, make it three hours. Do you still stick to that? And my next question is going to be: When do you intend to file, if any, your motion for rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do intend to file that and I have to check on what that estimate, that must have been, I hope it was, the estimate for direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the estimate for direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the Busina witnesses, and I hope we can do it relatively quickly. They are all very straightforward witnesses. And we do have a couple of other witnesses in mind, and I know Mr. Thayer is working on that as we speak. We are watching some issues as they arise during the direct and cross-examination of this witness as well, but I don't see any longer than a week, I hope. We're also discussing with Mr. Zivanovic this issue that has continued to be their outstanding motion for records for ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to decide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because we are -- what we have been kicking around is the idea of providing ICMP DNA records for the some 30-plus Busina victims; since we now know they've challenged that, we had no idea there was a challenge when it came up in court initially, but trying to get ICMP to give them those DNA records for those cases and if they want, we can bring in Mr. Parsons with a DNA person to be cross-examined on those records and maybe that will save the issue of the motion or if you -- if you if you make a ruling on the motion, maybe the whole thing will change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The ruling on the -- on Mr. Zivanovic's motion will be handed down pretty soon. It's practically ready, we are just going through the last draft. So we should be able to hand down the decision fairly quickly, possibly even this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But apart from that, what is more of concern to us at the present is when to expect the motion for rebuttal from your side or any other similar motion because you seem to indicate also the possibility of a similar motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We -- I can get back to you very soon on that. As you know, we've just withdrawn the idea of two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is something that is priority for us, and I will discuss this with Mr. Thayer and we'll get back to you -- well, probably the best information will be for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. That would avoid us having to fix a time limit, which we wouldn't like to do. The other thing I just wanted to mention en passant, which I'm sure you will think about and act upon is the following: As I said, time is flying, and very soon we will come to the end of the Pandurevic defence case. We'll come to the end of the reopening of the Prosecution case, and possibly rebuttal, and rejoinder, if there is one; and there we also will be finding ourselves faced with a decision on how much time to grant for the final briefs, et cetera. I would like you, as we have done before, to meet, have consultations amongst yourselves, and then come back to us with your suggestions which we will keep in mind when we are taking a decision later on. If you can actually come back to us, say, not later than next week, I think it would be very useful to us. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just on this particular issue from the defence side, we've already have -- we had those consultations already, and we have a joint position with only one of the defence teams having a slight different position on one issue; and we've communicated this information to the Prosecution and we hope to sit down with the Prosecution as soon as possible so that we can inform the Trial Chamber with, hopefully, a joint position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And since there is no ban for such meetings during the weekend, I suggest that you try and come back to us as early as possible next week. Okay. Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you for being patient. Yes, Mr. Pandurevic, I'm sorry I didn't notice you straight away. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to apologise to Mr. Bourgon if he took any of my answers personally. Secondly, I would like to thank him for his fair treatment of me and his general approach during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't think I will meet socially with Mr. Pandurevic over the weekend, but I do agree. Thank you. So Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. I would first like to ask you this. In July 1995, you knew Vujadin Popovic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Between your return from your mission on the 15th of July, 1995, and the end of that month, do you remember seeing him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear from anyone else that he was in Zvornik or in the Zvornik area at the time? But please, limit yourself to any knowledge that you might have had at the time and do not conflate this with something that you might have learned at a later stage while, for example, listening to proceedings before this Tribunal or reading Mr. Butler's report.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard at the time that Mr. Popovic was in the area, that he appeared at the Zvornik Brigade command and that he was in the Zvornik municipality area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was part of the information that I received from Obrenovic which he, in turn, had received from Jokic, indicating that Jokic had seen him at the command, I think the same day that he saw Mr. Beara. Nevertheless, Obrenovic received information from Mr. Trbic too indicating that on the 16th, Trbic saw Mr. Popovic in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told anything specific on that occasion as to what he did or what he was doing generally?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing very specific. His name was dropped during a conversation about all the general activity surrounding the POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "all the general activities" is there anything more specific you'd like to share with us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing that would be more specific than everything that has transpired during this trial. In the sense of those people arriving in the Zvornik area and then being kept in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of January, you spoke about a meeting that took place at the Bratunac Brigade on the 11th of July, 1995. Page 30883, line 16 to 30884, line 11, that is the transcript reference. I think it's line 11. You spoke about a meeting that was held at the brigade. General Mladic was there, General Krstic, as well as the commanders of a number of other units. You do remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember if on that day, General Mladic or anyone else for that matter said that the 28th Division was not in Srebrenica at all but rather somewhere along the Sarajevo front line?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one said that the 28th Division was in Srebrenica. We had entered Srebrenica by this time and all we knew was the possible axes for the withdrawal of the 28th Division. However, at an earlier stage, there was information indicating that certain individuals were leaving the Srebrenica area including a number of commanders and possibly minor groups being sent to the Sarajevo front as reinforcements, but I can't be more specific about the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at 3038, it's an OTP document, P3038. If we look at the header of this document, you will see that it says Republika Srpska, and then we can't see which specific body produced this document. We can see the number, the date. I think you are probably familiar with this document. At least now you are, even if you didn't see it at the time, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have come across this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "before," do you mean back in 1995 or do you mean during this trial?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean during this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the lower half of the document, and could we please lower the document -- or rather the bottom of the B/C/S page. You will see that the time is recorded there that the document was received, the time the telegram was sent, the 11th of July, 1995 at 1945 hours. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, received, processed at 1947 and received 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, 1945. The meeting that you held at the Bratunac Brigade was some time later, I think you said it was past 2200 hours in the evening; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was an order given at the meeting for the units to deploy and wait for a possible return of the forces of the 28th Division from the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those of us who were involved in Krivaja 95 operation received no orders about any possible involvement vis-a-vis the units of the 28th Division that were on their way back from the Sarajevo front.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You received no information like this at the meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know or do you perhaps remember if the information was generally known that the commander of that division, Oric, and possibly other officers were outside Srebrenica at the time when Krivaja 95 was in progress?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, we knew that he was not in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an assumption that he was in the Sarajevo front somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could counsel please be asked to speak up or move closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the fact that I had no information like that at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I had no information on the possible presence of the forces of the 28th Division on the Sarajevo front. Earlier we had received word that Naser Oric was in the Tuzla area. I don't know if he was in the Sarajevo area at the time or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, the interpreters are complaining that your voice is too low, and it's not reaching them properly. So if you could either approach nearer to the microphone or raise your voice a little, that would help. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, there was no doubt at the time, was there, that up until the 11th of July, when the VRS came in, the 28th Division had been in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us something in very general terms about the discipline of the soldiers of the VRS, and I'm quoting the relevant portion of the transcript for you, specifically, first you talked on the 11th of February, 31300, lines 24 to 31 301, line 3. I'll read back to you what the transcript recorded: [Previous translation continued] ... [In English] "... what is that all about? "A. That was probably to the third of the people that were supposed to be sent to the Djevanje-Kruske area because that was the problem with that particular battalion when a man has to be sent outside the defence area." [Interpretation] You mentioned something that was generally similar to this in your evidence on the 13th of February, 2009, 31407, that is the page, lines 10 through 17. You say: [In English] "Mr. Bourgon, I have to touch on your previous question. I did my very best to protect the lives of my men and to ensure that my soldiers had what they needed. These were reservists who did not understand the logic of warfare and the ways in which the soldiers were used. They were local patriots. Had they carried out my orders and acted in ways described by certain individuals in this courtroom, and had everything been done the way they say it was, I would happily have been a commander for another ten years, but that's not how it was." [Interpretation] Can you please clarify some of the things that you've told us already? First of all, they were only reservists in the Zvornik Brigade, there were no soldiers waiting to be trained; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no recruits and no soldiers serving their regular military term, reservists alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you said when you said they were local patriots?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot has been said about that during the trial as well as about the front and the defence lines resembling the skin of a leopard in terms of pattern but each of soldiers were prepared to defend their own doorstep or stand around the fringes of their own village in order to protect it, and they were not prepared in keeping with the military rules and norms to get involved in a different area militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That means that you and other officers were facing some difficulties whenever you had to convince them to follow orders; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was often necessary to go and talk to those units and explain why their presence was required elsewhere. They would have been glad to accept any mission as long as it was within their own area, place of residence, as opposed to leaving their native area and being dispatched elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume they knew that they were under every obligation to carry out any orders from their superiors, they had been appropriately trained and aware of that, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who did their regular military term in the JNA were well familiar with the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Surely everyone knew that they mustn't commit any war crimes or any crimes at all even if ordered to do just that; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How familiar were they with the provisions of international law of war? That is to say the least debatable. My opinion is they were entirely unfamiliar with those. Based on human reason, they could have assumed what would have been legal and what would have been illegal and which category murder would have fallen under as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Back at the command, you had an organ for operations and training; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about that organ? Was it not supposed to explain different rules and regulations to the soldiers that they were meant to abide by including this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not their job. The operations and training organ has an entirely different job. We would receive from the Main Staff and the corps command instructions on the application of the Geneva Conventions and norms of International Laws of War. The officers were familiar with those. Now, as for officers in lower-ranking units and to what extent they familiarised their foot soldiers with these rules and regulations, that is really not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would they brief their superiors about what exactly they did and what they told their soldiers about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there's an order that is sent from the brigade command or some sort of an information letter to the battalions and other units, are received by those units; and those units are duty-bound to act on that. One analyses any missions completed, and everyone submits reports in relation to their own area and any steps taken within their own area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: About what I've just asked you about the operations and training organ, was that perhaps a responsibility of the other organ, moral and legal affairs, or rather morale and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who could have forwarded information like that to the lower-ranking units, it could have been the operative organ it could have been the morale people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you monitor this as a commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information were forwarded down to units, but to what extent it went downwards through the battalions, companies and eventually to the privates. I don't know the details but the feedback information always came that they were informed; however, it was not often easy to finish this whole job entirely due to the absence of soldiers from their positions for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a couple of things relating to the wounded who were at the clinic of the Zvornik Brigade. You spoke about this on two occasions on 9 February, that's page 31144, line 19 to 31149, line 31, and then again on the 10th of February, 2009, page 31169, line 15, up to 31170, line 5. From your testimony given on the 10th of February, it seems that Obrenovic had informed you about the wounded people in the Zvornik Brigade clinic and that he did it on either the 18th or the 19th of July at the IKM; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure whether this was exactly what was said. I would kindly ask you to quote my words from the referenced page numbers in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That actually starts from line 15, I apologise: [In English] "When I returned from the IKM, I can't tell you exactly when it was, whether that was on 18th or 19th because I don't remember. However, as soon as I received the information, as soon as I learned that there were such people there, I was not really clear why the wounded had to be accommodated in the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade together with the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade who had been wounded, and I personally ordered Dragan Obrenovic to inspect them and to look after their safety and that order should be conveyed to the medical personnel. My order was to treat the enemy wounded as any other wounded person would be treated." [Interpretation] My question in this regard is: Did Obrenovic tell you that these wounded men had been brought at the time when you were absent?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the time was, but I think it was mentioned that they had arrived a few days before I learned about it, whether it was precisely before the 15th, I cannot confirm. Anyway, I learned about their presence exactly as you have quoted my words just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This infirmary and the whole medical service of the Zvornik Brigade was not part of the staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. This was the medical service within the logistic department of the Zvornik Brigade, and the chief of the medical service was responsible for the infirmary and for providing accommodation to the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Obrenovic had an opportunity and a right to issue orders or instructions or guidelines to the chief of medical service as a deputy commander not in the capacity of a Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could have issued him tasks even in the capacity of the Chief of Staff provided these tasks were in the spirit of my previous orders and decisions. In addition to that, I had personally entrusted him, and that is Dragan Obrenovic, with taking care of and providing accommodation for these wounded men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Dragan Obrenovic tell you that he had made any other requests prior to receiving instructions from you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so other than that he only knew that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that a usual practice for patients who are not members of the VRS to be moved from a civilian hospital to the infirmary of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is outside any existing rule and defies any military logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had an opportunity in this courtroom to hear the testimony of Dr. Zoran Begovic, who was the chief of the medical service; and he was practically running the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade. He testified on the 21st of March, 2007. Among other things, and I refer you to page 9137, lines 17 to 21 where he says that 10 to 15 wounded men sometime in July 1995 arrived at the Standard barracks from a hospital in Zvornik. It was obvious they had received some prior medical treatment and that they had been registered with the medical institution from which they had arrived. However, they said that they arrived there without any notification being sent to the staff in the infirmary including the head physician. Tell me, did you hear from Obrenovic or anyone else, and whether it was customary to bring anyone to the infirmary without notifying the infirmary staff in advance?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we have urgent delivery of wounded soldiers from our unit or from the veresa [phoen] in general, they are admitted immediately and taken care of, so there could be no notification. However, speaking about this specific incident, I believe that the command of the brigade should have received some kind of order and then it will be -- it will make arrangements for these people to be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
