utterances.text: Dr. Begovic also said on page 9142, line 10, to page 1144 [as interpreted] line 8 to the effect that a group of soldiers had brought these wounded men to the infirmary. My question is: Did Obrenovic tell you who those -- these people were, this group who sent them there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did. I don't know who had brought these people and put them there. By the way, an infirmary is medical institution where people who are injured, who are sick, and who have sustained light wounds are accommodated for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction. Line 6, page 49, the page should be instead of 1144 [as interpreted], 1143, line 8. I'll repeat on page 49 of today's transcript, line 6, instead of 1144, it should read 9143.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm also going to read one section of his testimony, I mean Dr. Begovic, before I ask you the next question. This is precisely from the pages that I mentioned a short while ago: [In English] "... by a number of soldiers; is that right? "A. Yes. "Q. Okay. Now, in relation to where they were taken after they were brought to that room, did you have any discussion with anybody concerning where they should be placed or where they would be placed? "A. When Mr. Dragan Obrenovic came, then he started talking. He said that they would be accommodated there, that was the safest place for them, that they would be secured by the military police, that was the only room where they could have been accommodated but because everything else was full; and I guess for their personal safety, it was a good idea to have police nearby. I guess that was the idea, but I don't know. "Q. Okay. And so from the area where you worked, they were taken to another room; is that right? "A. Yes, correct. "Q. Did you have to make any special accommodation, move things or make arrangement in order to have those people placed in that room? "A. No, nothing was moved. There were palettes there, and then boards, and then mattress were placed on top of that, soft mattress." [Interpretation] That was it, more or less. My question is: Is it in a way customary or do you as a commander find it unusual that Dragan Obrenovic was the one who made decision as to when and where these wounded persons would be accommodated depending on the severity of their wounds and the need for receiving medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he had full insight into their medical condition. Anyway, he was not qualified to do that. In my view, that should have been done by the chief of the medical service. As for security measures to be put in place, that was the job of Dragan Obrenovic. The treatment falls into the category of medical profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, Dr. Begovic said on page 9144, lines 6 to 14 that he had heard from Obrenovic that the doctors from the Zvornik civilian hospitals would be coming over to treat the wounded Muslims. Now, was that customary to make such arrangements not to be made through the chief of the medical service and the medical staff, but instead, they just hear that this had been agreed between, in this case, the Chief of Staff and some of the doctors from the hospital in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what Mr. Begovic has said, but to me, this looks like a rather unusual arrangement and an unusual way in which these wounded men appeared in the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade. When they were transferred from the hospital in Zvornik, it would only have been logical for the chief of the medical service to go to the hospital beforehand and to check with the doctors there what kind of wounds these men had sustained, to review the medical records, and then admit these men. Had this been done in that way, maybe Begovic would not have granted permission for them to be accommodated in the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did Obrenovic ever tell you or inform you about this kind of arrangement or this kind of agreement with the staff of the Zvornik hospital?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never mentioned anything to me to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Begovic also testified that Obrenovic had told him that he shouldn't enter these wounded men in the register of the patients that's being kept in the infirmary of the Zvornik Brigade. Tell me, is that within the remit at all of the Chief of Staff or the man who was standing in for you to make such a decision and instruct the medical service not to register the patients in their books?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This boils down to direct meddling with the procedure and the professional conduct. This shouldn't have been -- should not have been told to Begovic. Begovic would have acted, as he did, in all the previous occasions and he would open and maintain proper records for those people as he did for all the other wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Begovic also said that he had received from Obrenovic instructions or an order to have temperature charts opened for those persons. Did Obrenovic ever tell you about this instruction that apparently he had given Dr. Begovic for the patients not to be recorded in terms of admission, and only to have temperature charts drawn up for them instead of the normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he told me nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you testified in chief --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to speak up, the interpreter didn't hear the names. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Zivanovic, back to square one. The interpreters couldn't hear the names that you mentioned. If you could repeat your question a little bit slightly more loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While testifying in chief, you spoke twice about Popovic and about the fuel which he had apparently requested. You saw some intercepts, you saw some materiel lists. The first time was on the 2nd of February, page 31014, line 19, and then all the way to the end of that day's transcript. The second time was on the 12th of February, 31318, line 18 and 31323, line 20 is in relation to the 16th of July, 1995. In addition to that, the 10th of February, 1995, page 31221, line 4 to 31222, line 12. This is Popovic's questions, the questions that you asked about fuel back in September 1995. Generally speaking, you agree that fuel was of exceptional strategic importance for the VRS at the time, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuel is certainly strategically important, but when you talk to me as a soldier, you mention strategically, strategic importance, what I mean is truckloads and truckloads and truckloads of fuel. That's the order of magnitude. But yes, in answer to your question, it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was very important to get fuel because of the sanctions; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't the one who was in charge of getting fuel, but I know that it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me and do you know at all that fuel was something that was often stolen, smuggled, resold, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the significance of fuel to the VRS, and given what you know about the areas of competence of certain bodies, were the security organs in addition to other things responsible for uncovering any such criminal activity such as the stealing of fuel and any form of misuse at all within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, when your expert spoke about the security organs and the rules of service pertaining to the security organ, I think one of the areas of competence was who was in charge and who they were working with. I think he also said that the security organs were contributing to the uncovering of crimes within certain units, and I think smuggling fuel would fall under one of those headings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke, among other things, about the rule of responsibility of the brigade and regiment commands; 7D717, as far as I remember. Among other things, I think it said that security organs did counter-intelligence work and took measures in order to uncover any acts of espionage and counter-intelligence activity. How did that relate to fuel and activity like that, the stealing of fuel, the stealing of fuel, then do you think that, according to these rules this would have been something for the security organ?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't as such a part of counter-intelligence work. As for subversion or internal attempts to undermine the established order, well that might be taken as one of the tasks for the security organ. Fuel expenditure and in other words how much fuel is used up, that is something for the chief of technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So he is watching how much fuel is used up and the security organs should see to it that the fuel is not stolen; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he sees thieves and potential danger everywhere, well, then, there would be more security officers than those looking after the technical department and using the actual technology available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, and in your understanding, was there any reason for anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it becomes clear that there has been theft, stealing of fuel, or expenditure levels that were not typical, anyone can report that, and the security organ should then be involved in the investigation. There is some form of material and financial monitoring. They look into all the books, and this is certainly not the job of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as a commander, did you ever notice any expenditure levels in terms of fuel that were not typical, anything that might have indicated some form of irregularity or anything that might have warranted action from the security organ, by the security organ?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have enormous amounts of fuel available to us to begin with. Such enormous expenditure levels would have cropped up if the armoured mechanised units were being used, but we knew what the daily needs were for fuel; and there was a procedure in place that was pretty much established on how fuel was handed out, how the travel lists and warrants were filled in and recorded. These were then sorted out on a monthly basis so sometimes minor theft was possible; for example, someone mis-recorded the time they spent on a mission, bad road conditions, bad traffic conditions, all vehicles, more fuel used up than envisaged by the regulations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard Branko Bogicevic testify here, didn't you, he was a member of your unit. You probably remember that, that was on the 18th of June, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard about the circumstances under which he transported fuel that had apparently been ordered by Popovic, who he got the order from, where he took this fuel to and what the circumstances were of the hand-over itself. Do you remember those details?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the evidence, but I'm not sure about each little detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to refresh your memory, this was on the 18th of June, 2008. The pages are 22364 to 22374, line 24. Based on his evidence, he took the fuel to Pilica. That was the order he had received from the technical department of the brigade. His orders were to hand over the fuel to some people who were waiting behind Pilica along the road to Bijeljina. The fuel was then poured from barrels into jerrycans. There weren't sufficient jerrycans to go around. There was a dispute, they wanted to take his barrel away, which he refused to allow them to do and that's how the 140 litres of fuel were spilled. There were no officers among those people there, otherwise if there was an officer ordering him to let go of that barrel he would have to do that because he was just an ordinary soldier. He said he didn't know Popovic at all, and the document that you were shown here was produced only after the fuel had already been handed over. And he was never told to begin with who to hand the fuel over to. Were those circumstances not indicate that there was some irregularities in terms of how one dealt with the fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he said that the document was produced following the hand-over of the fuel, that means one knew exactly who the fuel was handed over to, and there must have been some sort of a record reflecting that. At any rate, based on the documents available to us, which is the record of this hand-over, one can see that the Zvornik Brigade dispatched 500 litres of D-2 fuel to the Drina Corps command, in parentheses, Mr. Popovic. The Zvornik Brigade from now on has nothing more to do with this fuel and cannot be held responsible for the way it is used. That is as much as we can infer based on the documents. Now, I really don't know what actually happened on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the question, isn't it? The documents could be forged because there's no other a way to steal fuel from an army; right? My question to you is what about the circumstances under which the hand-over occurred. Do they in any way indicate to you about what happened to the fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one thing is certain, that this was certainly not the best way to forge this, you know, by stating that they actually handed it over to 2nd Lieutenant Popovic, who was the security chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me one thing, did you ever see that document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there must be thousands and thousands of such materiel lists in the logistics unit of the Zvornik Brigade. I never signed a single one myself or indeed set eyes on any of them. Perhaps I did when I went back to the logistics units where they had their offices but the orders were signed by the commander for logistics, each and every one of them, and the remaining officers in the technical department, the traffic department, the quartermasters department and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll return in 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to make a correction in the transcript it is page 56, line 16. The B/C/S word, "vraceno" was translated as "spilled" instead "returned."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in relation to what you called excessive use of fuel, something that could perhaps be noticed, you didn't have that problem, you didn't noticing anything like that happening in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally have access to that type of information but had someone informed me about any excessive use of fuel or fuel disappearing, I don't think anything like that ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that in your regular --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be instructed to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, again, and if you could repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also try not to overlap because you were moving a little bit too fast, in my opinion, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that in your regular combat reports, you regularly reported on the daily use of fuel to the Drina Corps command; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your observation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now please look at your own regular combat report or rather that of the Zvornik Brigade, the date being the 13th of July, 1995, P325. Can we look at paragraph 6? We can't actually see it in the B/C/S, not in it's entirety, so maybe we could just lower this. Yes. Paragraph 6 says: "Logistic support is functioning with difficulty due to a shortage of fuel, ammunition, and all calibres and spare parts." We're just focussing on fuel here. What is shown here is the consumption of fuel D-2, 412 litres?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with that. Can we now please go to the next regular combat report, 328. 326, I'm sorry. This is P326, an OTP exhibit. We can go to paragraph 6 again. It reads: "Logistic support is functioning with difficulty due to a shortage of fuel, ammunition of all calibres and spare parts." Consumption, D-2, 827 litres. You agree; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 is nearly identical in all regular combat reports. The fuel consumption is not always accurately expressed. It's always shown as being slightly more than is actually consumed in order to try and obtain from the corps any amount of fuel at all. The consumption is calculated on a daily basis based on reports that arrive from the units and also based on what the traffic and technical department issued and used up over a day's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, can we conclude that on the 14th of July, the amount of fuel used up was three times that used up on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. Maybe this much was actually issued. I'm not sure if it was actually all used up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, and you should know, was there any peculiar going on on the 14th that would have required a bigger amount of fuel than usual?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, combat activities, ambushes being set up, people were being driven to and fro, perhaps a greater number of different activities than on the previous day, the 13th; but we also know that certain engineering machines on that day were beginning to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice this discrepancy between the 13th and the 14th in terms of how much fuel was used up?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read the report at all. Therefore, I never took note of the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us why you did not read the reports at all, those pertaining to the 13th and 14th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hardly ever read the reports except the ones that I signed. When I was there, I would have a glancing look and I believe I have explained sufficiently here where I went when I came on the 15th and when the first time was that I returned to the command. These reports were history by then especially as compared to what was soon to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please go back to 328, report 328. I think the previous reports were dispatched by Obrenovic. Can we please again go to paragraph 6. It's on the next page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is rephrased to some extent, it reads: "Logistic support is functioning with difficulty due to reasons already given." Again, there is a chart showing the use of various items. Again, the amount of fuel, 841 litres. Can you explain why this particular day, the consumption was twice as great as on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that the tank company had its manpower levels brought up, the one that had returned from Zepa on that day, hence the greater-than-usual amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to 7D532.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, your regular combat report dated the 16th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7D532.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 6 again: "Logistics support is functioning with difficulty due to reasons already known," yet again "and there are breakdowns in communications." D-2 consumption, 2.595 litres. Did you notice a jump up in the consumption of fuel in relation to the previous day?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well this is best compared to the materiel lists where you can see fuel being supplied to the units. You can see the lists recording the issuing of fuel at the various petrol stations and the travel lists. The 16th was a very demanding day. What purpose this amount of fuel was used for, I don't know. It is possible that the fuel was delivered to the users, and that day it had left the petrol stations, and it was recorded as consumption. If you go back to the documents I have mentioned, if you analyse them, it should be easy enough to establish what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could even do that, but my question is this: You, in your capacity as brigade commander at the time, did you notice this jump in fuel consumption between the 13th and the 16th, 400 litres to begin with and ending at 2.500 litres over a single day. Did you perhaps not consider that to be excessive in terms of fuel consumption?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea how much fuel had been used up on that day. The traffic clerk or rather the chief, Mr. Pantic, had the best, most reliable information, and I believe he would be able to explain this. It is possible that some materiel had been brought up over from the logistics bases on that day, some other supplies coming in and being delivered such as food or something along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you drafted this combat report and when you dispatched it, did you pay this information any heed at all, how much fuel was being used up, fuel consumption in relation to the previous day, for example, three times as many?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was drafted by the duty operations officer, and he dispatched it at the time given here. You know where I was at the time. I hadn't seen the report. I hadn't read the report, and I hadn't signed the report, and I had no idea how much fuel had been used up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, perhaps, see the report two, three, four days later; did you ever read those reports that other people drafted?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because you didn't read those reports at all, the reports that we discussed and that we'll keep on discussing, or is it just that you skipped some reports?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you see a report that I actually signed, I read those. Some in their entirety and some I just glossed over, as we say. Those not signed by my hand were not read, not on the day when they were dispatched, not later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you deny that you produced these reports at all?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I wasn't the person who produced the draft of this report. The interim combat reports that we discussed were indeed dictated by me. The duty operations -- the operations duty officer is the person who produced regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the reports for the 15th and 16th of July, did you ever read those?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now go to that same report in relation to the 17th, P331.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Zivanovic, but before the report comes up, I just remembered something. Around that time, I think on the 17th of all days, the 17th and the 18th to be more specific, some gravel and pebbles were taken to Baljkovica, a container arrived and some other things were being tidied up and sorted out; so that might have accounted for the use of that amount of fuel, that amount of fuel being issued or used up on that day or sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who exactly brought the gravel there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your brigades?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trucks from our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go to P332 now, please. Have a look, sir. 331. Can you see this here, fuel consumption, 1.590 litres in this case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't read this combat report either, did you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, you said someone was in charge of all this fuel. I assume that to be one of the commander's duties, was that assumption correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander is a commander, and everybody says so. And a commander is in charge of all sorts of things. I don't keep track of how much fuel is used up, but I am in charge of all the decisions on how my units are used and how the combat equipment is used; and there has to be a military rationale behind all of these decisions. If I find out that there is theft, that people are stealing, it is my duty to put a stop to that or rather to prevent that. In the brigade, there are various kinds of services or bodies that are directly involved in jobs like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just clarify how exactly you thought you might find out about any stealing or misuse of fuel if you never read the combat reports that bore your signature?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you there was a procedure in place and our fuel was issued. I had a rough idea of when fuel got there and how much. I knew when a knew request was being dispatched asking for more fuel. Sometimes I could have my suspicions in terms of anything dodgy going on or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For example, do you know how much fuel was requested at the time by the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 16th or the intercept, I hadn't known. Pantic asked himself, and we were lucky that Pantic himself was in the traffic service and was well acquainted with officers over at the Main Staff who were in charge of fuel and also over at the corps. He would often wrap up these jobs all alone in terms of how fuel was obtained and supplied. I would normally not interfere at all because he was offering other types of services such as military vehicle maintenance over in Zvornik and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you knew that, didn't you, that he was offering various other types of service, other people's vehicles over in Zvornik and that's why he was being awarded more fuel.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't other people's vehicles, those were military vehicles but there were fewer garages in Han Pijesak than in Zvornik, and that's why he helped them out sending their vehicles to our garages, or he could enlist assistance like companies who will get the repairs done assuming there was a proper compensation, obviously; but everything was done under the strictest of procedures and this was nothing exceptional whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So why was he awarded any fuel at all just because of that or was he?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't because of that. The person in charge of distributing fuel faces a list of units and then they prioritise what goes to whom and in what order exactly. There is no violation involved. Pantic for example, is his friend, okay; so Pantic will get his supplies as part of the next round, and there is another person maybe on that same list who will just have to wait for a couple of days, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I want to get this man's role straight, Pantic. He just asked for some fuel but he couldn't have any idea about what the needs of the brigade might be in terms of fuel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part counsel's answer for the same reasons as mentioned before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a unit is used in combat and when there is an order by the commander, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, you are going too, too fast. I can hear it in the interpreter's voice. He is trying to do his utmost, but I'm sure he is suffering. So slow down, both of you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel also be asked to speak up, appreciably. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, again -- I mean I would understand it had it been Mr. Ostojic with his size, but in your case, I mean you should have no problem in keeping near enough the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I repeat my question or could you perhaps answer straight away?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need, I can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's really for the transcript. We need it for the transcript if you can kindly repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that Pantic could have requested the fuel that was necessary. It wasn't his call to assess what the brigade's needs might be because it was you, the commander, who was in charge of that and that was part of your tasks within the brigade and all the other officers. So he just did what he was told to do; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, yes, you're right. When a commander takes a decision on how the brigade should be used, then there is this paragraph that says logistic support. The amount of fuel is determined there as well as the amount of ammunition that may be used up for that particular mission. The circumstances under which we worked were peculiar, and we could not really move away from our defence area. We knew approximately what our daily needs in terms of fuel might be and despite this, we never received the exact amounts that we had requested. And whenever we got anything at all, or what we had requested, it would never quite meet our needs or exceed our needs. Pantic could always submit requests, and he was happy whenever he could report back to me that fuel had been received without me being involved in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were not involved in the process of actually making requests vis-a-vis the fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever a unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Pandurevic. The interpreters didn't hear the last part of your question, Mr. Zivanovic. Can you also switch the other microphone as well in case that is possible. Maybe that will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does your last answer mean that you did not participate in issuing requests for fuel? You did not get involved in deciding on the quantities of fuel necessary for the execution of daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those were just regular daily tasks, then the supply of the units would be regular and nothing out of the ordinary. There was no need for me to decide anything. It was well known how many vehicles were used every day, and they were the ones using the fuel. In case there was combat going on in the area of the brigade or outside of it, then it was well-known how many non-combat vehicles were engaged, how many combat vehicles were engaged, and then the fuel for the particular tasks had to be planned; and I had to be aware of the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like on the relevant dates, the dates that were covered by the regular combat reports that I've shown you, the 15th, the 16th, the 17th, for example? To be more precise, from the moment when you returned and took over the command of the brigade, did you issue any requests? Do you remember were there any fuel requests? Were there just regular fuel requests or were the quantities involved higher than normal?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of those days, in addition to the regular supply, there was also increased supply due to combat activities due to the fact that units were brought in and taken from the area and that fuel was issued daily on request of the units that were engaged and had to be supplied from our reserves. I never received a report talking about a lack of fuel which prevented the execution of a task and that was enough for me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that period, did you have any special requests for increased quantities of fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure Pantic did send such requests because he had realised how much fuel was issued in the course of a day and as soon as that was done, he asked and requested for his supplies to be replenished to cover the needs over the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, this did not have anything to do with any requests of your own?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were requests that you could see in the duty officer's log book. It says in that log book: At the end of the day, requests from the units listing the quantities of fuel requested by each of the battalions, and that's just one type of consumption. Another type of consumption is for the vehicles that served the logistics. Pantic was one who served those vehicles, he did not have to cover that with any requests, any prior requests. He just fuelled the vehicles that were used for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when it comes to that period how much did the brigade receive in terms of fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to inspect the lists, the receipt lists, I would be able to tell you how much fuel was supplied to the Zvornik Brigade in July and how much was consumed. I really can't tell you off my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've never had an opportunity to inspect those lists?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen a huge number of such lists here, all sorts of lists delivery books, receipt books, the books recording the fuel issued and so on and so forth, but I don't have the figures at my fingertip. I simply can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look together as how things stood, the number of the document is P290 and the page is 219, so I would like to call that document up on e-court, please. I can see that this is a list of fuel issued. Could this be blown up just a little for the benefit of everybody in the courtroom. In the left corner, you can see that the date is 15 July, I believe that this was filled out either in Han Pijesak or Vlasenica, it doesn't really make a difference, and I suppose that this is the date when the issuance of that fuel was approved?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the right corner, you can see another date, the 16th of July and also there is a number next to it, a number of a document, I suppose. I suppose that this is the date when the fuel actually arrived in the brigade. And we can see that the -- on the 16th of July, a total of 1.000 litres of diesel was delivered. Am I right in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the date 16th of July is the date when this list was accounted for and recorded into the books of the Zvornik Brigade, and the fuel arrived on the same day when it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you can look at the lower part of the document where you can see the signature of the person who received the fuel, there is also a stamp of the Zvornik Brigade, and above that, there is another date, the date is the 17th of July. Could that be the date when the fuel was accounted for in the book, of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. This was sent to the accountant, this list, this copy of the list, and the first date is the date when the fuel was recorded by the logistics organ because it really did not take the fuel two days to get from Vlasenica to the Zvornik Brigade, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like us to look at page 216 in the same document. Again, in the left corner we can see a date. This time it is the 16th of July, and the date is repeated in the right upper corner; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And we also see that the fuel in question is diesel, D-2 and the quantity is 2.000 litres; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again it was received by the same person. There is some other details featured in the document. Do you agree that this could possibly have been the fuel which was subsequently mentioned in the intercept, the two tones that had been sent to Zvornik on the 16th of July and from which the 500 litres that you mentioned were taken?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we make a link between the intercept, the note made by the duty operations officer, this particular materiel list, and the materiel list featuring 500 litres of D-2 then we can infer the following, Mr. Basevic requested from someone in the Zvornik Brigade to issue 500 litres of fuel. That person refused to issue the fuel and then that person was encouraged by saying -- by saying to Basevic, I'm sending you 2.000 litres so you can easily issue me with 500. The list featuring 2.000 litres arrived in Zvornik, the Zvornik Brigade was issued with 2.000 litres; however, at the same time, the Zvornik Brigade issued 500 litres to the command of the Drina Corps and writes the 500 litres off its books which means that it is left with 1.500 litres of fuel. In other words, this means that the Zvornik Brigade did not receive 2.000 litres on this particular occasion, but rather 1.500 litres that were accounted for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could just have a clarification. There may be a translation error because I thought I heard the General say that Zvornik was sending Basevic 2.000 litres, and that doesn't seem to make sense. That's what's on the transcript. I may be wrong, but it doesn't seem to make sense so it might ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Mr. McCloskey. Will you deal with that, Mr. Zivanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please repeat. You mentioned Basevic and the whole situation about the sending of the fuel to somebody. Could you repeat what actually happened? Was it Basevic who sent fuel or was he the one who received it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say both, Basevic sent 2.000 litres to the Zvornik Brigade. Previously, he had requested from the same brigade to issue 500 litres to the command of the Drina Corps, so what happened, the Zvornik Brigade did receive 2.000 litres, at the same time it issued 500 litres to the command of the Drina Corps which means that the -- what the Zvornik Brigade received on that day was 1.500 litres of fuel and not 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of one thing. You noticed in the materiel list that 140 litres of fuel were returned. Could you please explain how was it that the Zvornik Brigade wrote off 500 litres from its books and 140 litres were returned to it which can be seen in that materiel list?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the corps command requested 500 litres. Five-hundred litres were sent accompanied with a materiel list. Whoever used the fuel was very rational and didn't use the whole quantity. He only used what he needed and returned the rest. And again, the Zvornik Brigade was made accountable of the 140 litres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the 500 litres were written off at the corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first quantity was 500 and then 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're speaking far away from the microphone. And turn the other one -- but he is facing the other side so turning the left-hand side microphone will not help much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, as you are looking at this, doesn't it come obvious to you that the 140 litres were stolen, and the 140 litres that were returned to the brigade; isn't that obvious to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever made a note on the materiel list that 140 litres were returned was also supposed to return the fuel to the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But still, the corps command was charged with the whole 500 litres. It did not change.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the list was filled out to accompany the fuel, 500 litres were requested and 500 litres were noted. However, that person actually received 360 litres. That's why the 500 is crossed and replaced by 360. This is what happened during the hand-over of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you think that this was a correct procedure that this is how things should have been done? That it was okay to show to the Drina Corps that all the 500 litres were used and keep the 140 litres?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the intention of that person, he would not have crossed the figure 500 and replaced it by 360. He would have left everything as it was and he would have taken 140 and kept it for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And who are you talking about? Who is that person who crossed? I'm not expressing my doubts about the person who returned the fuel, I'm doubting the intentions of the person who kept the fuel for himself and you are talking about the person who returned the fuel and recorded it very honestly on the list.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about manipulance in the true sense of the word, people who were mishandling and misusing the fuel. Nobody actually stole 140 litres of fuel. It was returned to the Zvornik Brigade, and the Zvornik Brigade had to justify the consumption of the 140 litres and as for the 360, the consumption of that quantity had to be justified by the Drina Corps. They were the ones who had to account for the use of that quantity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood it, the Zvornik Brigade had all the 500 litres written off in favour of the Drina Corps. That's how I understood it, and that's why I am inferring that the 140 were covered up, stolen, and you are denying that, you are saying that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you saw the list which shows 360, so the valid number is 360 and not the crossed out number 500 litres. I'm really -- I don't know what the problem is. What's not clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you what's not clear. Where are the 140 litres? You are saying that that was not misused and stolen. Did this quantity enter the books of the Zvornik Brigade ever?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to be entered in the books because the Drina Corps could not take it off the books. If they received 500, that's what they accounted for. If they received 360, they accounted for the usage of 360, and the rest was accounted for in the books of the Zvornik Brigade. The Zvornik Brigade was charged with the remaining 140 litres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? Have you ever seen any document to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's written --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's written that the Drina Corps has no longer the liability for 500 litres.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says 360.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says that the brigade has no liability regarding 500 litres, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, this is not what is written there. What is written there is 360. Let us look at this list on the screen. I don't want to talk about it without looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, if your client wishes to speak to you, then you can approach him. I would prefer that rather than have him speak across the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, in future, if you wish to speak to your lawyer, please address the Chamber rather than speak loud across the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise on behalf of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us please now look at page 218 of this same document. Here, we can see that another 2.000 litres were received on that day by your brigade. It seems that this document is identical with the previous one. If we look, we can see the same signature of the recipient; however, if we compare the numbers next to the date, that is in box 1, and box 16, to the numbers in the previous document, we can see, first of all, that in the left top-hand corner there is the number 21/6-723 and then in the right-hand corner, there is 21/1-2148; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only I don't know which numbers were on the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can go back now to document 216. I'm sorry, page 216. The same document. We can see now that the number is 21/6-718 and on the right, it's 21/1-2150.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, can we conclude from this that on the 16th of July, the Zvornik Brigade received a total of 5.000 litres of fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the materiel list that arrived at the Zvornik Brigade established exactly the amount of the fuel that arrived and reached the brigade. It might be 5.000. It might be more. But it has nothing to do with the materiel list showing the 360 litres that were given over to the Drina Corps. Maybe it was taken out of this quantity of 2.000 or the other quantity of 2.000. It's irrelevant. The point is that the Drina Corps had these 360 litres instead of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you think -- is it important what happened with 4.460 litres that the Zvornik Brigade had?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's important. The Zvornik Brigade was using this fuel according to its needs, and it's covered with appropriate documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen this document, I presume, naturally?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see each and every document. I don't know whether the point of this exercise is to establish how the Zvornik Brigade used up its fuel or how and for what purposes these 360 litres were used up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 360 litres of fuel can be traced when and where it was issued and we even know if any activities were going on at the time. What I'm interested in now, on the 16th of July, when these 4.640 litres were delivered to the Zvornik Brigade, can you tell me were there any specific activities going on that required such a huge amount of fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That probably had to do with replenishment. It wasn't only in this month that we received 2.000 litres. Our monthly requirements were much higher than the quantities received and shown here. You could see from daily report if the minimum amount was 400 litres, if you multiply that by 30, that's 12 tons a month. So you shouldn't be surprised that this kind of quantities were supplied, 2.000 plus 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm noticing is that the 4.000 or more precisely 4.200 litres were used in only two days of the 16th and the 17th. Are you talking about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go back, if you wish, to the regular combat report of the 16th and the 17th so we can add up exactly the quantities that we are discussing. First, the 16th of July, 7D -- I'm sorry, give me just a moment for it. 7D532 is the document. We see here too 2.595 litres?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P331.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well let me just tell you about the 16th of July. This represents the consumption before the 2.000 litres arrived, because this is a summary report for that particular day. You don't honestly believe that these 2.000 were immediately dispatched on the ground and used for something. It was sent to the pump and only the quantity received previously was used up and this is the replenishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So how do you know all this if you didn't monitor the situation with the fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the date when the fuel was dispatched and received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the fuel was received, at what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let us assume that it was received at 5.00 in the morning, which was impossible and the amount was 2.000 litres, how was it possible that the consumption was 2.500, who used all this fuel? This amount of fuel arrived on the 16th and was stored at the pump and the report for the 16th represents the consumption of the fuel received earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What you want to say is that this fuel was actually used up on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see the date is the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do and as I understand it, this is an exact quantity of fuel used up on that day; but I have the impression that you're trying to tell us something else, that this is not exactly what is represented here?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the fuel issued from the pump, whether it was completely used that day is a separate issue, and this is not the fuel that arrived on the 16th that you are talking about. And even if that were the case, what happened with those 360 litres? I have no answer to that, whether these 360 litres were used up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you do have an answer about the consumption of the 4.460?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see that from the documents of the Zvornik Brigade. We had books in which each vehicle and each journey was registered every day. There were requests coming from units. There were working lists. There were receipts and issuing papers. There is a whole set of documents that can show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand fuel is important, but if he could put his case to the witness on this so we can see where this is going because it's impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd support that, and I also think it's a little discourteous when a witness says can we discuss the question you're asking with the document on the screen, not to put it up for him to let him see it and comment on it. It's page 220 of P290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, I mean, you've asking questions on this fuel business for an hour plus. You're being called past now and asked what is the purpose of this line of questions. What is your case, in other words? What are you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The issue of fuel was put to the witness during his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And also some relation of my client to the fuel and relation of duties of security service of VRS regarding fuel and regarding protection of the Army of Republika Srpska from subversive activities, from stealing of fuel, and all other kinds of abuse of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said counter-intelligence, I wasn't far off the mark because that's how we started in the first place, whatever the relationship. Yes, we've got five minutes left. Mr. Haynes, do you insist on the point raised by you or can we move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, if I think it's necessary, I can deal with it in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed then, then conclude for the day, Mr. Zivanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to see my last question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last question was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, tell me just one more thing. Now that you said that this quantity was not used up on that day, is that your assumption or are you positive about this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really going to drive me into the logistics department. I never said that, as you put it, this used-up quantity of that day -- this report says that this is the consumption for that particular day, but it refers to the fuel issued from the pump station, and there's documents to corroborate that. During that same day, however, they received another quantity of the fuel, and it was stored at the pump station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is very clear and it goes like this: Since you know that there was a report from the pump, did you ever raise the question of issuing 2.595 litres to someone? Didn't you ask to which unit it went?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This quantity was issued on that day. At that point, there was seven battalions, there was a Podrinje detachment, a tank company, there was at least six or seven vehicles on the move on that day, and this fuel was issued to them. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that done with a view to carrying out combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the combat activities and the overall activities that the brigade was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can stop here. We'll continue tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
